title: BALAAM COULDN’T CURSE THEM—SO HE TAUGHT THEM HOW TO DESTROY THEMSELVES
paragraphs: BALAAM COULDN’T CURSE THEM—SO HE TAUGHT THEM HOW TO DESTROY THEMSELVES

The terrifying connection between Numbers 25, Numbers 31, and Revelation 2 reveals something every Christian fighting temptation needs to understand: when the enemy cannot defeat you from the outside, he may try to seduce you into surrendering from within.
There is something deeply unsettling about the story of Balaam.
Not because a donkey spoke.
Not because a pagan diviner stood on a mountain and looked down upon the tents of Israel.
Not even because a frightened king desperately wanted God’s people cursed.
The most disturbing part comes later.
Because Balaam discovered something terrifying.
If Israel could not be cursed from the outside, perhaps Israel could be corrupted from the inside.
And suddenly this ancient story stops feeling ancient.
Because some of the most devastating spiritual defeats do not begin with persecution.
They begin with invitation.
A conversation.
A private message.
A glance that stays too long.
A relationship you already know is pulling your heart away from Christ.
A browser opened when nobody is watching.
A compromise you promised would happen only once.
A secret appetite you keep feeding while still singing worship songs on Sunday.
Nobody had to drag you away from God.
Something simply became attractive enough that you began walking away yourself.
That is why Balaam’s story should make every believer pay attention.
Balak, king of Moab, was terrified of Israel. He summoned Balaam because he wanted supernatural help against the people God had blessed.
But Balaam could not simply manufacture a curse against the will of God.
Again and again, blessing came from his mouth.
Israel appeared protected.
The enemy wanted them cursed.
God would not permit it.
And you might expect the story to end there.
It doesn’t.
Numbers 25 suddenly takes us somewhere darker.
Israel is staying at Shittim, and Scripture says the people began committing sexual immorality with the women of Moab. The women invited them to sacrifices offered to their gods. Israel ate.
Then Israel bowed.
Then came one of the most chilling sentences in the chapter:
Israel “joined himself unto Baalpeor.”
Notice the descent.
Sexual compromise.
Participation at the table.
Idolatry.
Bondage.
What looked like appetite became allegiance.
What began in the body reached the soul.
The Hebrew language of Numbers 31 later pulls back the curtain even further.
Moses says:
“הֵן הֵנָּה הָיוּ לִבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל בִּדְבַר בִּלְעָם לִמְסׇר מַעַל בַּיהֹוָה עַל דְּבַר פְּעוֹר...”
Hen hennah hayu livnei Yisrael bidvar Bil'am...
The crucial phrase is בִּדְבַר בִּלְעָם — bidvar Bil'am.
It means, in context, “through the word/counsel of Balaam.”
Numbers 31:16 identifies Balaam as connected with the counsel by which Israel was led into unfaithfulness concerning Peor.
Now something that Numbers 25 did not initially explain has been exposed.
There was strategy behind the seduction.
And centuries later, Jesus Himself makes the connection unmistakable.
Speaking to the church in Pergamum in Revelation 2:14, Christ says that some among them held:
“τὴν διδαχὴν Βαλαάμ”
tēn didachēn Balaam—
“the teaching of Balaam.”
Then comes the explanation:
“βαλεῖν σκάνδαλον...”
balein skandalon—
to place a stumbling block before Israel.
And what did that stumbling block involve?
“φαγεῖν εἰδωλόθυτα καὶ πορνεῦσαι”
phagein eidōlothyta kai porneusai—
to eat things sacrificed to idols and to commit sexual immorality.
There it is.
Numbers 25 shows the fall.
Numbers 31 reveals Balaam’s involvement.
Revelation 2 explains the strategy.
Balaam could not successfully curse what God had blessed.
So the trap became compromise.
And that is where this story becomes painfully personal.
Because Satan does not always need to convince you that God does not exist.
Sometimes he only needs to convince you that one hidden sin does not matter.
He does not always need you to renounce Jesus publicly.
Sometimes he is satisfied when you keep calling Jesus “Lord” while privately making peace with something Jesus died to free you from.
That is far more subtle.
And far more dangerous.
Still know worship songs.
Still quote Scripture.
Still tell people, “God is good.”
Still attend church.
Still own three Bibles.
Still know exactly when to say “Amen.”
And yet there can be one room inside your heart where you have quietly hung a sign:
Jesus, You can have everything except this.
That room may be pornography.
An affair.
Lust.
Bitterness.
Greed.
An ungodly relationship.
Secret conversations with someone who is not your spouse.
Alcohol controlling you.
The approval of people.
Money.
Pride.
An obsession.
An unforgiving heart.
Or some habit nobody knows exists because you have become extraordinarily good at appearing spiritually healthy.
That is why this story hurts.
Because Balaam’s strategy was not merely about getting people to break a sexual rule.
The sexual sin was tied to something deeper.
Worship.
Numbers 25 says they were invited to sacrifices, ate, bowed down, and attached themselves to Baal of Peor.
The real battle was ultimately over allegiance.
And that remains true today.
Sexual sin is never merely about sex.
Greed is never merely about money.
Pride is never merely about ego.
Addiction is never merely about appetite.
Every sin eventually asks the same ancient question:
Who will rule you?
And sometimes the most dangerous idols are not statues sitting inside temples.
They are desires sitting inside us.
That is why Jesus’ words in Revelation are so serious.
He was not speaking to pagans outside the church.
He was speaking to a church.
People who carried His name.
People living in a hostile environment.
People who had endured pressure.
Yet Christ still confronted compromise among them.
That should humble us.
Because surviving persecution does not automatically mean we have defeated temptation.
You can be courageous in public and compromised in private.
You can defend Christianity online and neglect Christ when the screen goes dark.
You can win an argument about morality while losing the battle for your own purity.
You can expose everybody else’s sin while carefully hiding yours.
And perhaps the hardest sentence in this entire article is the one you already know:
God sees it.
Not the edited version.
Not the explanation.
Not the excuse.
Not the version your family believes.
Not the version your church friends see.
God sees what happens after midnight.
He sees the deleted conversation.
He sees the second account.
He sees what you search.
He sees what you fantasize about.
He sees what you keep returning to.
He sees the relationship you know you should leave.
He sees the bitterness you secretly enjoy rehearsing.
He sees the compromise you renamed “struggle” years ago because calling it sin would require repentance.
And yet...
He sees something else too.
He sees you.
Not merely your scandal.
Not merely your failure.
Not merely the worst thing you have ever done.
He sees the sinner Christ came to save.
This is where the Gospel changes everything.
Because Christianity is not the announcement that good people managed to keep themselves clean.
Christianity is the announcement that Jesus Christ came for sinners.
The same Bible that exposes sin announces a Savior.
Jesus did not come merely to make immoral people behave better.
He came to reconcile rebels to God.
He lived the righteousness we could never produce perfectly.
He carried sin to the cross.
He shed His blood.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
The answer to Balaam’s ancient trap is not merely stronger willpower.
It is Christ.
The answer to shame is Christ.
The answer to guilt is Christ.
The answer to slavery to sin is Christ.
The answer to the believer who has fallen and wonders whether there is any road home is still Christ.
But grace is not permission to remain chained.
Grace calls us out.
Jesus does not say, “Your sin doesn't matter.”
He offers something infinitely better:
Forgiveness.
Cleansing.
Freedom.
A new Master.
A new heart.
A new direction.
Repentance means we stop defending the thing that is destroying us and turn toward the One who can save us.
Maybe that is why you are reading this right now.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe you have begged God for forgiveness so many times that you are ashamed to pray the same prayer again.
Maybe you have promised, “Never again,” and then found yourself back in exactly the same place.
Maybe your greatest fear is not that somebody will discover your secret.
Maybe your greatest fear is that you will never change.
Hear the Gospel.
Your hope was never your ability to become your own savior.
Your hope has a name.
Jesus Christ.
Run to Him honestly.
Bring the ugly truth.
Confess it.
Stop protecting it.
Cut off what continually leads you toward it.
Seek mature Christian accountability.
Open Scripture when your appetite tells you to open the door to temptation.
Pray before temptation becomes negotiation.
And when necessary, seek trustworthy pastoral or professional help rather than fighting alone in secrecy.
Because secrecy gives sin somewhere to breathe.
Confession drags it into the light.
Perhaps you have fallen badly.
Perhaps your story contains adultery.
Pornography.
Promiscuity.
An abortion.
Sexual brokenness.
Betrayal.
Years of secret addiction.
Or choices you would give almost anything to undo.
The Gospel does not require you to pretend those things never happened.
It declares that your past does not possess greater saving power than the blood of Christ.
There are consequences we may still have to face.
Relationships may require rebuilding.
Trust may take time.
Some scars remain.
Grace is not pretending damage never happened.
Grace means damage does not get the final word.
Jesus does.
That is our heartbeat at Gospel Warrior:
Not because the scandal was imaginary.
Not because sin is harmless.
Not because repentance is optional.
But because the cross is real.
The tomb is empty.
And Jesus Christ is still transforming sinners.
So be honest right now.
Not with me.
With God.
What is the thing you keep allowing near your soul because you are convinced you can control it?
What compromise keeps whispering, Just once more?
What relationship keeps weakening your obedience?
What secret would terrify you if somebody opened your phone tonight?
What appetite has slowly begun demanding your worship?
Balaam’s story is thousands of years old.
The trap is not.
Maybe your enemy cannot make you stop believing in Jesus.
So temptation tries something quieter.
It asks you to believe in Jesus while slowly learning to live without obeying Him.
Don't confuse God's patience with His approval.
Come home.
Someone reading beneath you may discover that they are not the only person fighting.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God.
It doesn't.
One share may put the Gospel in front of someone who would never walk through the doors of your church.
There may come a night when temptation sounds more convincing than it does today, and you may need to remember again:
The enemy does not need to curse you if he can persuade you to compromise.

And if Gospel Warrior has been helping you grow in Scripture, conviction, repentance, healing, and faith in Jesus Christ, stay close by following this ministry and inviting your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelieving friends to follow along for daily biblical truth and encouragement.
It does not.
And never because anyone should be pressured into giving.
Scripture says giving should come from a heart that has decided freely, “not reluctantly or under compulsion.”
If your desire is to glorify God with the resources He has entrusted to you, prayerfully consider whether supporting Gospel Warrior should be one expression of that stewardship.
Pray.
Read.
Grow.
Send this article to someone fighting quietly.
Jesus did not purchase you with a monthly payment.
He purchased His people with His blood.
And perhaps that is the final lesson Balaam never wanted Israel to remember.
The people of God did not need another curse to destroy them.
They needed only to forget whose they were.
So tonight, before you close this article, remember whose you are.
If you belong to Jesus, your secret temptation is not your lord.
Your appetite is not your lord.
Your past is not your lord.
Your shame is not your lord.
Jesus Christ is Lord.

And the same Christ who exposes what is killing you is the Christ who calls you out of darkness, receives the repentant sinner, cleanses the guilty, restores the broken, and teaches His people how to walk in the light.
Balaam may have understood how to build a stumbling block.
But he never possessed the final word over the people of God.
Neither does your scandal.
Neither does your failure.
Neither does the night you wish you could erase.
The enemy may remember the chapter where you fell. Jesus is still writing what comes after it.
